descripcion: Some English verbs are always followed by one particular preposition, and that preposition is not chosen by logic — it is part of the verb. *Depend* is always followed by *on*, *listen* by *to*, *wait* by *for*. These cannot be worked out from Spanish, because Spanish picked a different preposition for many of the same verbs: *depender de*, not *de* → *of*. At B1 the goal is to learn the highest-frequency pairs as single units — *depend on*, *arrive at* — instead of treating the preposition as a free choice made at the moment of speaking.

filas: I listen to music every morning.
We arrived at the station. / We arrived in Berlin.
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: Some very common verbs take no preposition at all: *discuss*, *enter*, *phone*.

ejemplos.texto: It depends on how much time we have.
I've been waiting for you for twenty minutes.
She asked for help, but nobody was listening to her.
We arrived at the airport at six and arrived in Madrid at nine.
Don't worry about the cost — it belongs to the company.

notas: The preposition is part of the verb, so learn them as one item: not *depend* plus a preposition, but *depend on*.
Spanish uses a different preposition for several of these verbs, so translating the preposition directly is the single biggest source of error here.
*Arrive* takes *at* for a point like a station or an airport, and *in* for a town or a country.
A few frequent verbs take no preposition in English even though Spanish adds one: *discuss the plan*, *enter the room*, *phone your sister*.

contraste.es: Spanish has a dependent preposition for most of these verbs too, so the concept itself is familiar — the problem is that the choice rarely matches. *Depender de* becomes *depend on*, *esperar a* becomes *wait for*, *pensar en* becomes *think about*. Because the pattern exists in both languages, Spanish speakers transfer it confidently and get the preposition wrong rather than omitting it.

errores: *It depends of the weather* — the preposition is *on*, not *of*.
*Listen the music* — *listen* always needs *to* before its object.
*Discuss about the plan* — *discuss* takes no preposition at all.
*Wait me* — *wait* needs *for* before a person or thing.
